children: By Nate Raymond

A Florida man has agreed to plead guilty to charges that he acted as a key middleman who helped facilitate what prosecutors say was a decade-long scheme in which attorneys used confidential information from their law firms to feed an insider trading ring tips about nearly 30 underway mergers.

Gavryel Silverstein, a Florida resident in the insurance adjusting business, agreed to plead guilty to conspiring to commit securities fraud and money laundering as part of a deal that was filed on Wednesday in Boston federal court.
He was one of 19 people who were arrested in May, when prosecutors unveiled indictments against him and others following a sprawling investigation. He is the third of the 19 to strike a plea deal.
Thirty-one people overall have been charged. Ten of them starting in 2024 pleaded guilty in secret as prosecutors were investigating the matter.

Prosecutors have agreed to recommend that Silverstein is sentenced at the low-end of the applicable sentencing guidelines, and he has agreed to forfeit $125,000 he derived from the scheme, according to the
Cara McNamara, a federal public defender representing Silverstein, did not respond to a request for comment.

Prosecutors allege that the insider trading scheme was orchestrated by Nicolo Nourafchan, who had worked at the law firms Sidley Austin, Latham & Watkins and Goodwin Procter, and personal injury attorney ​Robert Yadgarov.

Prosecutors said Nourafchan, while working at the law firms, beginning in 2014 tipped Yadgarov and others off to impending corporate transactions in exchange for kickbacks generated from any trading profits.

Nourafchan and Yadgarov also recruited other attorneys into the scheme to feed tips to them, including one who worked at Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz and another who was employed by Weil, Gotshal & Manges and Willkie Farr & Gallagher. Both men had pleaded not guilty. None of the law firms was accused of wrongdoing, and prosecutors consider them victims.

Prosecutors and the US Securities and Exchange Commission say that Silverstein and Nourafchan were close friends who grew up together. Authorities said Silverstein during the scheme acted as a middleman, passing along tips to others to trade on in exchange for kickbacks that would be shared between him, Nourafchan and Yadgarov.
Nourafchan and Yadgarov have both pleaded not guilty and are awaiting trial.
The case is United States v. Fejal, US District Court for the District of Massachusetts, No. 1:26-cr-10133.
For the United States: Kaitlin O'Donnell of the US Attorney's Office for the District of Massachusetts
For Silverstein: Cara McNamara of the Federal Public Defender Office
